ai.title: Cardiovascular Medicine
ai.subject: Medicine
ai.summary: A concise guide to evaluating and managing common cardiovascular disorders in low‑resource settings, focusing on bedside reasoning, essential investigations and urgent care.

b: Identify chest pain, dyspnoea, palpitations, oedema, syncope.
Use bedside auscultation, pulse assessment and simple bedside ECG if available.
sections.p: Cardiovascular medicine covers diseases of the heart and blood vessels diagnosed by history, physical exam and basic tests.

b: NYHA I‑IV based on symptoms with ordinary activity.
TIMI 0‑7 predicts 30‑day mortality in acute coronary syndrome.
sections.p: Severity is graded by functional class (NYHA for heart failure) and by acute risk scores (e.g., TIMI for ACS).

b: Hypertensive heart disease – leading cause of LV hypertrophy and failure.
Rheumatic heart disease – valve stenosis/regurgitation, common in young adults.
Coronary artery disease – increasingly seen with urbanisation.
HIV‑associated cardiomyopathy – dilated heart in advanced disease.
Malaria or severe anaemia – high‑output failure.
sections.p: In East Africa the most frequent aetiologies are hypertension, rheumatic heart disease, coronary artery disease, HIV‑related cardiomyopathy and malaria‑induced anaemia.

b: Acute dyspnoea with crackles → pulmonary oedema.
Elevated JVP, hepato‑jugular reflux → right‑sided failure.
Chest pain radiating to left arm → possible ACS.
Irregular pulse, absent atrial kick → atrial fibrillation.
sections.p: Patients may present with breathlessness, peripheral oedema, chest discomfort, palpitations or syncope, often with a background of known risk factors.

t.b: Assess haemodynamic status; low BP suggests shock, high BP suggests hypertensive emergency.
Detect ischaemia, arrhythmia, conduction block; ST‑elevation → urgent reperfusion.
Look for cardiomegaly, pulmonary congestion, pleural effusion; normal size does not exclude early failure.
Identify LV function, pericardial effusion, IVC collapsibility; if unavailable, rely on clinical signs.

t.a: Full blood count and malaria smear
t.b: Detect anaemia, infection; severe anaemia can precipitate high‑output failure.
Assess renal function, myocardial injury; troponin rise supports ACS but may be normal in early infarction.

b: Chest pain with diaphoresis or hypotension → possible myocardial infarction.
New‑onset severe dyspnoea with pink frothy sputum → acute pulmonary oedema.
Syncope with arrhythmia → high risk of sudden death.
Rapidly rising JVP with muffled heart sounds → cardiac tamponade.
sections.p: Recognise features that demand urgent referral or transfer.

b: Hypertensive emergency: IV labetalol or nicardipine; avoid nitroglycerin if right‑sided failure.
Acute coronary syndrome: aspirin, clopidogrel, and if PCI unavailable, give streptokinase; avoid fibrinolysis in recent bleeding.
Heart failure: loop diuretic (e.g., furosemide) for congestion; ACE inhibitor for remodeling; avoid NSAIDs.
Rheumatic valve disease: refer for surgery when severe; give penicillin prophylaxis to prevent recurrence.
Arrhythmia control: rate control with beta‑blocker; avoid digoxin in hypokalaemia.
sections.p: Treat the underlying cause first, then provide supportive measures.

b: Blood pressure target <140/90 mmHg; use thiazide diuretic if ACE inhibitor unavailable.
Statin therapy for secondary prevention of coronary disease.
Regular echocardiography when feasible to track valve function.
Vaccination against influenza and pneumococcus to reduce decompensation.
sections.p: Long‑term care focuses on risk‑factor control and monitoring for disease progression.

b: Pulmonary tuberculosis causing pleural effusion → may be mistaken for right‑sided failure.
Severe anaemia from malaria → high‑output failure, not primary cardiac disease.
Pericardial TB → constrictive pericarditis can look like right‑sided failure.
sections.p: Conditions that mimic cardiac disease in low‑resource settings.

b: Normal ECG does not exclude early myocardial infarction; rely on clinical picture.
Chest X‑ray may be normal in early heart failure; look for peripheral signs.
Troponin can be elevated in severe malaria or sepsis without coronary occlusion.

whenToSeekHelp: Sudden chest pain with sweating or faintness
Severe shortness of breath with cyanosis
Syncope with palpitations or new murmur
Rapidly worsening oedema or abdominal distension
